item.title: Physics-Based TCAD Modeling of Nanowire Cryotrons with Coupled Superconducting and Thermal Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanowire cryotrons (nTrons) provide gate-controlled superconducting switching, current gain, and high-impedance outputs for cryogenic computing, detector readout, and superconductor-semiconductor interfaces. We develop a physics-based Sentaurus TCAD framework that couples time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau dynamics, separate electron and phonon energy equations, and mixed-mode circuit simulation. Superconducting terminal-current corrections connect the custom solver to the native electrical solution, linking local suppression of superconductivity, heating and cooling, and current redistribution in the external circuit. To our knowledge, this is the first Sentaurus-based mixed-mode TCAD implementation for nTrons. We calibrate the model against experimental switching data at six gate currents using a single parameter set. The model achieves an RMS load-current error below 1 $\mu$A outside the switching region and switching-current differences of about 1 $\mu$A or less. Simulations show that a center gate gives the highest switching sensitivity, while a drain-side gate gives the largest post-switch resistance. Narrower channels switch at lower currents and exhibit higher resistance. Transient and bidirectional bias sweeps capture electrothermal hysteresis, gate-controlled switching latency, and bias-controlled recovery. Simultaneous activation of three gates lowers the switching threshold from about 104 $\mu$A with all gates inactive to about 12 $\mu$A, demonstrating cooperative suppression of superconductivity. The framework supports the design of nTron geometries, operating conditions, and multi-input architectures.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah All Hasib, Md Shafayat Hossain, Ahmedullah Aziz, Shamiul Alam

item.title: Pseudospin-mediated broadband hypersonic phonon transport beyond localized Berry curvature
item.description: arXiv:2611.34077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phononic nanostructures offer compact and highly confined control of elastic waves for signal transport, filtering, and quantum transduction. More recently, topological phononic structures have been explored as a route to robust waveguiding around defects and sharp bends, offering a promising basis for scalable and reliable phononic circuitry. However, how robust transport can persist as conventional localized Berry-curvature signatures diminish with increasing structural perturbation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate bend-resilient hypersonic phonon transport beyond the conventional valley Hall framework. Using an engineered propeller phononic crystal operating at 1.9 GHz, we continuously increase the geometric perturbation to gradually weaken the valley topology while enhancing modal pseudospin character. Strikingly, as the Berry curvature progressively delocalizes from valleys, the complete elastic bandgap broadens to a normalized width of 34% and the interface modes become more strongly confined. Two-port electromechanical measurements on a thin-film lithium niobate-on-SOI platform experimentally confirm broadband interface-mode transport with no measurable bend-induced loss, despite the absence of well-localized valley-topology signatures. Our findings establish modal pseudospin engineering as a powerful design principle for robust acoustic guiding beyond conventional topological constraints, paving the way for broadband hypersonic phononic circuitry for classical and quantum information processing.
item.dc:creator: Byunggi Kim, Michele Diego, Yohei Ogawara, Matteo Pirro, Hyuga Oka, Ryo Sasaki, Satoshi Iwamoto, Masahiro Nomura

item.title: Mathematical modeling of regime-dependent thermal response in multilayer wall assemblies with equal total steady thermal resistance
item.description: arXiv:2611.34087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Steady thermal resistance is a fundamental characteristic of building-envelope assemblies; however, equal steady resistance does not uniquely determine their transient thermal behavior. This study aims to numerically separate the effects of layer order, temperature-dependent thermophysical properties, and redistribution of thermal resistance between bulk and interfacial components in stationarily equivalent multilayer wall assemblies subjected to periodic and finite-pulse thermal loading. A one-dimensional transient heat-conduction model with Robin boundary conditions, finite interfacial thermal resistance, and source-supported temperature-dependent material properties was employed. All compared configurations were constrained to the same total steady thermal resistance at the reference temperature, $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 3.65315$ m$^2$ K/W. The numerical implementation passed the adopted verification procedure with restrictions. The combined grid/time uncertainty was 0.325 %, below the prescribed 0.5 % acceptance criterion. For the tested pair differing only in layer order, the relative effect was -0.905 % for the periodic decrement factor and +0.566 % for the finite-pulse peak transmission ratio, with effect-to-uncertainty ratios of 79.2 and 88.9, respectively; the opposite signs therefore refer to two distinct regime-specific metrics. The temperature-dependent configuration produced a numerically resolved periodic effect of -2.005 %, whereas the corresponding pulse effect of -0.282 % remained below the adopted numerical-resolution threshold. For a compensated 5-10 % redistribution of bulk thermal resistance to interfacial contacts, the additional dynamic effect was likewise unresolved. The results demonstrate the value of controlled factor separation combined with explicit numerical-uncertainty assessment when evaluating transient thermal behavior.
item.dc:creator: Dmytro Usenko, Valery Usenko, Iryna Usenko

item.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.33450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.
item.dc:creator: Xiaodong Luo

item.title: Infrared-absorption magnetometry in a diamond nanocavity: demonstration and limits at the nanoscale
item.description: arXiv:2611.33481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently. Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate, for the first time, singlet-absorption magnetometry using spin-dense diamond nanocavities. By probing cavity modes near the 1042 nm NV singlet transition, we observe spin-dependent cavity transmission and perform cavity-enhanced magnetic field sensing. We further develop and experimentally validate a model that accurately predicts the spin-dependent cavity response, describes the optimal operating conditions, and identifies the practical limitations of different optically detected magnetic resonance modalities. Together, these results establish cavity-enhanced singlet absorption as a scalable readout mechanism for integrated diamond quantum sensors and provide a practical framework for engineering next-generation nanophotonic diamond quantum magnetometers.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas J. Sorensen, Elham Zohari, Chris Coutts, Sean McNaney, Matteo Feder, Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Sigurd Fl{\aa}gan, Vinaya K. Kavatamane, Christoph Simon, Paul E. Barclay

item.title: A scalable dense silicon qubit architecture with logical operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33590v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires a large number of physical qubits to encode logical qubits with sufficiently low error rates. Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform because of their small footprint, compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing technologies, and demonstrated high-fidelity operations. However, realizing a scalable architecture that supports quantum error correction, qubit transport, wiring, and logical gate operations remains a major challenge. Here, we propose a scalable dense silicon spin qubit architecture designed to support large-scale FTQC. The architecture consists of qubit memories, data qubit lanes, and cross junctions. Qubit memories store logical qubits encoded using the rotated surface code and support logical single-qubit operations. Data qubit lanes enable high-speed one-dimensional spin shuttling for connectivity between logical qubits, while cross junctions provide routing functionality and implement transversal logical CNOT gates. Using experimentally demonstrated silicon spin qubit parameters, we evaluate logical error rates as a function of code distance and estimate that a code distance of at least 21 is required to achieve logical error rates below $10^{-10}$ per syndrome cycle. We further analyze wiring constraints based on CMOS-compatible multiplexed control schemes and show that, with optimized wiring efficiency, more than 120,000 logical qubits could be integrated on a 100 mm $\times$ 100 mm chip. These results provide a practical roadmap toward large-scale FTQC based on silicon spin qubit technology.
item.dc:creator: Masahiro Tadokoro, Tetsuo Kodera

item.title: Remote and Noncontact Acceleration and Suppression of Heat Convection on Object Surfaces using Intensity-Adjusted Acoustic Streaming
item.description: arXiv:2611.33752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The temperature of objects in an environment is often controlled by accelerating or suppressing heat convection. Conventional methods generally involve insulation for heat retention and forced convection for cooling. However, there is no practical method for remotely and target-selectively controlling heat convection in objects in room environments. In this study, we demonstrated that intensity-adjusted acoustic streaming (ultrasound-driven airflow) can both suppress natural convection and induce forced convection on the surface of a heat source. The direct acceleration and deceleration of air over the object surface were induced by an ultrasonic beam with high temporal and spatial resolution. The experiment showed that it is possible to switch between insulating and cooling by adjusting the ultrasonic output intensity, and that it is essential for heat retention to prevent heat from escaping from the object surface by convection using acoustic streaming. We consider these results to lead to the realization of a situation where virtual heat-retaining blankets or cooling fans that are customized for specific objects in the environment can be ubiquitously attached to them, opening the door to applications such as temperature control of food and beverages and remote control of temperature profiles in manufacturing processes and laboratory settings.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Yuzawa, Keisuke Hasegawa

item.title: Ultrasensitive, universal single-ion nanodetector
item.description: arXiv:2602.00406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, a carbon nanotube (CNT) based single-ion detector is proposed and its performance is evaluated with atomistic quantum transport models. The sensor can detect any ion type without molecule-specific functionalization and allows for continuous real-time ion monitoring. A single ion temporarily changes the operating principle of the sensor's CNT field-effect transistor into a resonant tunneling diode. The concrete device example of this paper showed a source-drain current increase of 5 orders of magnitude induced by a single ion.
item.dc:creator: Namita Narendra, Tillmann Kubis

item.title: Interaction-Free Polarimetry
item.description: arXiv:2207.13539v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The combination of interaction-free measurement and the quantum Zeno effect has been shown to both increase the signal-to-noise ratio of imaging, and reduce the energy absorbed by the imaged object. So far, however, it has not been used for quantitative polarimetry, the reconstruction of a sample's Mueller matrix. In this paper, we extend this to the polarimetry of diattenuating samples. For polarisation components that the sample strongly absorbs, the protocol identifies the sample with far less absorbed energy than a single-pass measurement, a benefit for delicate samples probed with high-frequency radiation. For weakly absorbing components the repeated passes through the sample absorb more, so the benefit is confined to strongly diattenuating features. A Fisher-information analysis shows that, for a sample with a lossless transmitting axis, the protocol locates the absorbing axis with far fewer absorbed photons than single-pass polarimetry, while it measures partial transmittances no more efficiently per absorbed photon, and that the same sorting of lossy components to one output port responds to retardance and depolarisation.
item.dc:creator: Shushmi Chowdhury, John Rarity, Jonte R. Hance

item.title: Chirality of a $\mathbb{Z}_q$ Model as Orientation-Odd Phase Shifts in Oscillator Networks
item.description: arXiv:2607.16606v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chiral interaction between discrete $\mathbb{Z}_q$ variables, which distinguishes clockwise from counterclockwise steps, arises in settings ranging from statistical physics to combinatorial optimization. When such an interaction is realized by continuous phases, however, its kernel fixes the phase coupling only at the $q$ grid points, so which part of the coupling carries the discrete chirality is not determined. We show that for any realization that matches the discrete values and treats a kernel and its mirror image alike, the kernel is chiral if and only if the coupling has a nonzero odd part, and that neither property of the realization can be dropped. Among the realizations that reproduce all discrete energies and equilibria, the one with the fewest harmonics is unique and satisfies the second property automatically, so that its sine components measure the discrete chirality exactly; a faithful realization with an even coupling, as in existing oscillator Ising and Potts machines, represents only nonchiral kernels. In the induced dynamics this odd part is an orientation-odd phase shift, which changes sign with the orientation of the coupling, in contrast to the Sakaguchi phase lag. In oscillator networks it is realized by direction-dependent delays, and mixed-level circuit simulations show that exchanging the delays reverses the chirality of the locked states.
item.dc:creator: Yi Cheng, Zongli Lin
